info.name: Equipment Cleaning Log API
info.description:
Take-home assignment — Full-Stack Engineer, Leucine.

A cleaning log for pharmaceutical manufacturing equipment with a field-level audit trail.

## How to use

1. Start the API: `npm run dev` (listens on http://localhost:4000)
2. Make sure the database is seeded: `npm run seed`
3. **Run the whole collection** (Collection Runner) — folders are ordered so each request sets up the next, and every request carries assertions. A green run is a working API.

Or step through folder by folder from the top.

## Auth

Login returns a signed **httpOnly** cookie, which Postman's cookie jar stores and replays automatically — there is no token to copy. Folder 5 switches from an operator to a supervisor mid-run, which is how the role checks are demonstrated.

## What is worth looking at

- **Folder 4** — the audit trail: one event per save, one line per field that moved, and no event at all when nothing changed.
- **Folder 5** — segregation of duties: an operator cannot verify their own work.
- **Folder 6** — keyset pagination, with an assertion that no row appears on two pages.

item.name: 4 · Cleaning records & the audit trail
item.description: The heart of the assignment. Run these in order: each one sets up the next.

request.description: `cleanedBy` defaults to the authenticated user but may name a colleague. Writes a `create` audit event in the same transaction.
Every field holding a value moved from nothing to that value. Fields still empty emit NO line — null → null is not a change, and the database CHECK constraint would reject one.

exec: pm.test('no line for a field that was never set', () =>

item.name: Update TWO fields in one save

request.description: One act by one person at one instant, affecting two fields — which is exactly why the audit trail is a header table plus a lines table.
Two events now. The update carries exactly two lines: one per field that moved, grouped under one actor and timestamp.
A user who opens the edit form and saves without changing anything. Succeeds, but must write no audit event: 'someone updated this' with nothing beneath it is noise a reviewer has to read past.
An explicit null CLEARS the field and must produce an audit line. Compare with omitting the key entirely, which leaves it alone. Those are different requests and the diff preserves the difference.

exec: pm.test('recorded as a change to null', () => {

item.name: 6 · Pagination
item.description: Numbered pages over LIMIT/OFFSET. The trade against a cursor — arbitrary access and a total, paid for with a COUNT and a scan past skipped rows — is in NOTES.md.

request.description: Every list endpoint takes page and pageSize and returns a pageInfo. One contract across the API.

exec: pm.test('served page 1 at the size asked for', () => {

request.description: The unique id in the ORDER BY is what makes this hold. Sorting on cleaned_at alone leaves ties in an arbitrary order, and a page boundary landing inside a tie can repeat one row and hide another.

item.name: Jump straight to the last page

request.description: Arbitrary access is the reason for OFFSET. A cursor names the last row seen, which is enough to go forwards and nothing else.

item.name: Page past the end is clamped, not empty

request.description: Page 9 of a 12-page list stops existing the moment the page size changes from 10 to 25. Returning the last page, plus a pageInfo saying which page that turned out to be, beats an empty grid the user has to diagnose.

exec: pm.test('and it actually has rows', () => pm.expect(b.data.length).to.be.above(0));

request.description: A caller that passes nothing gets page 1 at the configured default size, not the whole table.

item.name: Filter and pagination compose — the count follows the filter

request.description: A total that ignored the filter would render the right rows under the wrong number of pages.
One place decides how much data a single request may return, so no caller can ask for an unbounded response.
Pages are 1-based. A zero is a bug in the caller, not a request for the first page, and answering it silently would hide an off-by-one.

item.name: Audit history is paginated the same way

request.description: Same contract on every list endpoint. No endpoint can return an unbounded set, even one that usually holds a handful of rows.

item.name: 7 · Validation & error handling
item.description: One error envelope throughout: { error: { code, message, details? } }. No stack traces, no SQL, no constraint names.

request.description: body-parser throws BEFORE any route or schema runs. Unhandled that becomes a 500, which blames the server for the caller's mistake. Translated explicitly.
Schemas are strict: a typo is reported, not silently dropped. Ignoring it would leave the caller wondering why nothing changed.
Enforced in the service layer, because now() is not immutable and PostgreSQL will not accept it in a CHECK constraint.

item.name: 8 · Retirement, not deletion
item.description: A hard delete would either orphan cleaning history or cascade it away. Both are wrong for an auditable system.
